instrument.question_text: What is the probability of an AI-caused catastrophe — an event, principally caused by AI, in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period — occurring by December 31, 2050, under each policy condition?
instrument.shared_background:
Background Information

Concern about large-scale harms from AI has grown substantially over the last few years. Leading developers, including Anthropic and OpenAI, have publicly acknowledged that their models could potentially contribute to catastrophic outcomes including through the proliferation of biological or chemical weapons or autonomous action in high-stakes domains.
In the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament in 2022, the following unconditional forecasts of a similar global catastrophe scenario caused by AI were made (p. 16):


The median forecast among Superforecasters was a 2% probability that an AI-caused catastrophe occurs by 2100.
Domain experts on various existential and catastrophic risks gave a median forecast of 12%.
Members of the general public gave a median chance of catastrophe by 2100 of 5%.
instrument.event_definition:
This outcome is defined as an event caused by artificial intelligence in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period.
Artificial intelligence is defined here as ‘the development of machines capable of sophisticated (intelligent) information processing’ (Dafoe 2018, AI Governance: A Research Agenda; see pg 5 footnote 2 for more).
We use the term “be the cause of death” to cover cases where AI is the direct or proximate cause of the deaths. For example, if a robot powered by AI kills 10% of all humans alive at the time within a 5-year period, that will count for this outcome. Alternatively, if AI, operating without direct human intervention, causes the launch of nuclear weapons that kill 10% of all humans alive at the time, that will also count for the purposes of this outcome. If that same incident does not kill 10% of all humans, but the subsequent nuclear winter does, that will also count for the purposes of this outcome.

We consider AI a “proximate cause of death” based on the “but-for” test. This means we are considering events that would not have occurred or would have counterfactually been extremely unlikely to occur “but for” the substantial involvement of AI within one year prior to the event. One way to think of this rule is if the AI involved in an event could have shut down unexpectedly without dramatically reducing the probability of the event, then the AI was not a proximate cause. For example, if AI is substantially responsible for creating a superweapon that causes the death of the relevant (large) magnitudes of people, this would count for the purposes of this outcome. If AI acts autonomously in an armed conflict context and causes the deaths of the relevant magnitudes of people, this would also count. However, AI would not be considered a proximate cause if the AI did not directly cause or enable the event to transpire. For example, an AI assisting in targeting a nuclear weapon would not be considered a proximate cause if humans could have launched the weapon anyway without AI assistance.


For fatality and population data, we will rely on broadly recognized sources of population data, such as Our World in Data, the Economist, the United Nations, etc.
Where these sources disagree in ways that would change outcome resolution, we will resolve using the majority opinion of a panel of experts in demographics and fields relevant to the specific catastrophe (e.g. epidemiology for a pandemic).
In order to resolve positively, the relevant 5-year period must end before the resolution date, and begin on or after December 31, 2025.
If reasonable people disagree about whether this event has occurred, this outcome will be resolved via a panel of experts.
instrument.causation_criteria: Direct or proximate cause, with a but-for counterfactual test and substantial AI involvement within one year prior to the event; full wording retained above.
instrument.shared_policy_conditions:
Horizon: every condition is implemented immediately and remains in force through December 31, 2050.
Frontier model: a model trained with more than approximately 10^26 FLOP, or a regulator-updated equivalent as algorithmic efficiency improves.
Unconditional. Forecast the world as you expect it to unfold, including AI policies you expect to be implemented.
Status quo. Assume no new, substantial AI policy is adopted in China, the US, or any other jurisdiction hosting a frontier model from today through December 31, 2050. Existing measures remain in force as they stand today, but nothing substantial is added. By "substantial AI policy" we mean reflecting similar or greater stringency compared to those listed in this survey. Note that this is conceptually distinct from Unconditional, for which you should forecast the world as you expect it to unfold, including AI policies you expect to be implemented.
Conditional. For each policy condition (P1–P5), assume that the relevant governing body implements the policy immediately and that it remains in effect through December 31, 2050. In making this assumption, try to hold other factors constant and treat the policy implementation as exogenous. In other words, do not assume that implementation of a more stringent policy implies that the world is — in fact — more risky. We want your forecast of how risk changes as a result of the policy's implementation, not vice versa.
instrument.selected_condition_text: Forecast the world as you expect it to unfold, including AI policies you expect to be implemented.

event_window.end_rule_exact: In order to resolve positively, the relevant 5-year period must end before the resolution date, and begin on or after December 31, 2025.
event_window.boundary_note: The question uses by December 31, 2050, while the resolution text says the five-year period must end before the resolution date. Both are preserved; no invented inclusive/exclusive reconciliation.
